Two years later, in 2014, DHS created the Deferred Action for Parents of 
Americans and Lawful Permanent Residents CDAPA”), which established a 
new deferred action program for parents whose children were U.S. citizens or 
permanent residents. The two programs were immediately challenged as a 
violation of the APA’s notice-and-comment requirement, leading to the Fifth 
Circuit s opinion in Texas v. United States excerpted and discussed in Chapter 
5. The Fifth Circuit held that the challengers to the program were likely to 
succeed on their claim that the DAPA memorandum was a substantive rule 
required to go through notice and comment under section 553. The Supreme 
Court affirmed by an equally divided vote, which meant that it issued no 
opinion in the case.
Regents arose out of the Trump Administration’s 2017 attempt to rescind 
the DACA program. The Attorney General advised DHS that the DACA 
program was unlawful. Relying on the Fifth Circuit’s opinion and the Supreme 
Court’s equally divided affirmance, the Attorney General contended that 
DACA possessed the same legal * * * defects that the courts recognized as to 
DAPA” and was “likely” to meet a similar fate. The Acting DHS Secretary, 
Elaine Duke, then issued a memorandum terminating DACA, relying on the 
Attorney Generals advice (Duke memorandum”). Duke reasoned, based on 
the Supreme Court’s and Fifth Circuit’s rulings, that the “DACA program 
should be terminated. Various affected parties (including the Regents of the 
University of California) challenged the rescission as, among other things, 
arbitrary and capricious under the APA, because it failed to consider important 
factors bearing on the decision. The District Court for the District of 
Columbia one of the courts in which a challenge to the rescission had been 
brought held that the “conclusory statements [in the Duke memorandum] 
were insufficient to explain the change in [the agency’s] view of DACA’s 
lawfulness. The district court, however, stayed its order for 90 days to permit 
DHS to reissue a memorandum rescinding DACA, this time providing a fuller 
explanation for the determination that the program lacks statutory and 
constitutional authority.” In response, the DHS Secretary, Kirstjen Nielsen, 
issued a new memorandum in which she “decline[d] to disturb” the Duke 
memorandum’s rescission of DACA (“Nielsen mem ora n Hum”) The Nielsen 
memorandum articulated various justifications for the rescission of DACA,
